body:
The Harappan urban tradition

The Harappan Civilisation, also called the Indus Civilisation, developed one of the earliest urban traditions in the Indian subcontinent. Its mature urban phase is generally dated to approximately 2600–1900 BCE. During this period, settlements such as Harappa, Mohenjodaro, Dholavira and Lothal displayed planned streets, substantial buildings, drainage arrangements and facilities for storing or transporting goods.

The civilisation is named after Harappa, the first major site of this archaeological culture to be identified. Harappa and Mohenjodaro are in present-day Pakistan, whereas Dholavira and Lothal are in Gujarat. Other important settlements include Kalibangan in Rajasthan and Rakhigarhi in Haryana. The distribution of these sites shows why the civilisation cannot be confined geographically to the valley of the Indus River.

Archaeological investigations at Harappa and Mohenjodaro established that their remains belonged to a previously unrecognised ancient civilisation. In 1924, John Marshall, then Director-General of the Archaeological Survey of India, announced its discovery. Archaeologists such as Daya Ram Sahni and Rakhal Das Banerji contributed to the identification of the settlements.

What makes a settlement urban?

Urban architecture involves more than the presence of large houses. It requires the organisation of buildings, movement, water supply, waste disposal and shared facilities. Harappan settlements provide evidence of such coordination through their streets, brick dimensions, building platforms and drainage networks.

  • Planned settlement: Streets and building plots followed recognisable arrangements rather than developing entirely without coordination.
  • Construction standards: Bricks were made in widely recurring proportions, indicating shared building practices.
  • Public infrastructure: Streets, drains, wells, reservoirs and substantial communal structures required coordinated construction and maintenance.
  • Domestic architecture: Houses contained courtyards, rooms, bathing spaces and, in some cases, wells and staircases.
  • Fortification: Some settlements and internal sections were enclosed by massive walls, although their exact functions cannot always be established.

Chronology and the limits of archaeological evidence

The Mature Harappan phase is not the entire history of every Harappan site. Earlier settlements existed before 2600 BCE, and occupation continued in different forms after 1900 BCE. At Dholavira, for example, the archaeological sequence extends beyond the mature urban period.

Knowledge of Harappan architecture comes mainly from excavated buildings and objects. The Harappan script remains undeciphered, so archaeologists cannot identify the function of every structure from contemporary written descriptions. A building described as a warehouse, palace or ritual structure may be an interpretation based on its plan and associated finds rather than a proven original name.

Built remains and historical interpretation are different. A brick-lined tank is an archaeological fact. Identifying it as a ritual bathing place requires additional evidence and may remain uncertain.

Prelims focus

  • The Mature Harappan phase is generally dated to approximately 2600–1900 BCE.
  • Harappa is in present-day Pakistan; Dholavira and Lothal are in Gujarat.
  • The Harappan Civilisation extended beyond the Indus Valley.
  • John Marshall announced the discovery of the civilisation in 1924.
  • The Harappan script has not been deciphered.
  • Trap: Do not treat every proposed function of a Harappan building as an established fact.

[Sources: NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 1, Bricks, Beads and Bones, pp. 1–2 and 19–24; NCERT, Exploring Society: India and Beyond, Class 6, Chapter 6, The Beginnings of Indian Civilisation, pp. 85–91.]

title: Harappan Architecture: The Beginning of Urban Planning in India

body:
The citadel and the lower town

Many Harappan cities were divided into distinct areas. At Mohenjodaro, the smaller, elevated western section is conventionally called the citadel, while the larger, lower section is called the lower town. The citadel was raised on substantial mud-brick platforms and was separated from the lower town by walls. The lower town also had fortifications.

The term citadel identifies a physically prominent and fortified part of the settlement. It does not prove that a king lived there. Some significant structures, including the Great Bath, were located in the citadel, but their precise use remains a matter of archaeological interpretation.

Fortification and internal divisions

A fortification is a substantial wall or defensive enclosure around a settlement or part of it. Harappan fortifications could have helped regulate access, protect against threats or environmental hazards, and separate important urban sections. Their appearance alone does not establish a particular military or administrative purpose.

The pattern was not identical everywhere. Dholavira had several fortified sections, whereas the elevated citadel at Lothal was defined by its raised platform rather than by a separate enclosing wall. The entire Lothal settlement nevertheless had a fortified perimeter.

Grid-pattern streets and standardised bricks

At Mohenjodaro, streets followed an approximate grid pattern, with many crossing at nearly right angles. This arrangement helped organise residential blocks and allowed drainage channels to follow the streets. The settlement appears to have been laid out before much of its building activity took place.

Harappan bricks, whether sun-dried or baked, commonly followed a standard proportion of length : breadth : height = 4 : 2 : 1. This ratio helped builders use bricks consistently across walls and other structures. Baked bricks were especially useful where greater resistance to water was required.

Standardised does not mean that every building everywhere was identical. Local materials, available resources and site conditions produced important variations, particularly the extensive use of stone at Dholavira.

Courtyard houses and privacy

Residential buildings at Mohenjodaro often had rooms arranged around an internal courtyard. The courtyard could accommodate activities such as cooking and domestic work while providing light and ventilation. Houses differed in size, and some had more than 1 storey, as indicated by surviving staircases.

Many houses show a concern for privacy. Street-facing walls at ground level commonly lacked windows, while entrances were arranged so that a person outside could not look directly into the central courtyard. This distinction between the public street and the private interior is an important feature of Harappan domestic architecture.

Bathing platforms were common, and some houses contained wells. Domestic wastewater could be channelled through walls into street drains. The presence of household bathing facilities does not mean that every residence had its own well.

Public and private space

Harappan settlements combined domestic rooms and courtyards with spaces serving wider urban needs. Streets and drains were shared infrastructure. At some sites, archaeologists have identified large structures that may have served storage or other collective purposes. The Great Bath at Mohenjodaro and the large open ground at Dholavira are prominent examples of spaces with possible communal significance.

However, archaeologists have not conclusively identified a standard Harappan royal palace or a large temple of the type familiar from later Indian architecture. Public importance must therefore be inferred cautiously from construction, location and associated material evidence.

Prelims focus

  • Mohenjodaro had an elevated citadel and a larger lower town.
  • Harappan bricks commonly followed the proportion 4 : 2 : 1.
  • Streets at Mohenjodaro followed an approximate grid.
  • Courtyard houses often restricted direct views from the street.
  • Lothal's raised citadel was not separately walled.
  • Trap: A citadel is an archaeological description, not proof of a royal palace.

[Sources: NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 1, Bricks, Beads and Bones, pp. 5–8; NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 4, In the Earliest Cities, pp. 33–35; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Archaeological Remains of a Harappa Port-Town, Lothal, Description, Tentative List entry 5918, consulted 23 November 2026.]

title: Harappan City Layout: Citadels, Fortifications, Streets and Houses

body:
Water management as part of town planning

The Harappans constructed facilities for obtaining clean water, using it in homes and removing wastewater. These facilities were integrated with streets and buildings. Their design shows that water supply and drainage were important aspects of urban planning, not merely additions to individual houses.

Wells and domestic bathing spaces

Mohenjodaro contained numerous brick-lined wells, with archaeologists estimating approximately 700 wells across the settlement. Some were associated with houses, while others could be accessed from outside a house. This distinction matters because a well within a building complex was not necessarily restricted to one household.

Many houses had a brick-paved bathing area. Wastewater passed through an outlet towards a drain. The widespread presence of bathing spaces helps explain why the Great Bath should not automatically be interpreted as an ordinary public bathroom intended to meet everyone's daily needs.

How the drainage network worked

In many areas, household drainage connected to a larger street network. A typical sequence was:

  1. Water from a household bathing area entered a small domestic drain.
  2. It could pass into a sump or cesspit, where heavier solid material settled.
  3. The wastewater then flowed into a brick-lined street drain.
  4. Street drains carried the water away through larger channels.

Drains were laid with a gentle slope so that water could flow. Main channels were often covered with removable bricks or stone slabs, allowing access for cleaning. Long channels also had arrangements for removing accumulated material. This shows that effective drainage required both construction and continuing maintenance.

The system was not confined to the largest cities. At Lothal, for example, drains were built with fired bricks even where houses used mud bricks.

The Great Bath at Mohenjodaro

The Great Bath is one of the most distinctive structures on the citadel of Mohenjodaro. It is a rectangular brick-lined tank measuring approximately 12 m by 7 m. Steps led down into the water from the northern and southern sides. Rooms and passages surrounded the tank, and a well was situated nearby.

The builders made the tank substantially watertight using carefully arranged bricks, gypsum mortar and waterproofing material that included natural bitumen. Water could be supplied and later removed through a drain. These features indicate deliberate planning for filling, using and emptying the tank.

Its unusual construction and location suggest that the Great Bath had a special function. Some archaeologists have interpreted it as a place for ritual bathing, while other interpretations have linked it to restricted or elite use. Neither function has been established conclusively.

The Great Bath is at Mohenjodaro, not Harappa or Dholavira. Its identification as a special tank is secure; its precise social or religious purpose is uncertain.

What the engineering tells us

A network that required individual houses to connect with public drains implies coordination between domestic construction and street planning. Brick-lined wells, sumps and accessible drain covers also demonstrate an understanding of durability and maintenance. These observations support the conclusion that Harappan settlements possessed organised civic infrastructure; they do not, by themselves, reveal the exact titles or powers of the people who supervised it.

Prelims focus

  • The Great Bath is located on the citadel at Mohenjodaro.
  • Its approximate tank dimensions are 12 m by 7 m.
  • It had stairways on 2 sides and provision for drainage.
  • Brick, gypsum mortar and bitumen contributed to waterproofing.
  • Domestic drains commonly connected with covered street drains.
  • Trap: Ritual bathing is an interpretation, not a conclusively established use of the Great Bath.

[Sources: NCERT, Themes in Indian History, Part I, Class 12, Theme 1, Bricks, Beads and Bones, pp. 6–8; NCERT, Exploring Society: India and Beyond, Class 6, Chapter 6, The Beginnings of Indian Civilisation, pp. 91–95; NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 4, In the Earliest Cities, pp. 33–34.]

title: Harappan Water Engineering: Wells, Covered Drains and the Great Bath

body:
Location and environmental setting

Dholavira is situated on Khadir Bet, an island in the Rann of Kutch in Gujarat. Its location in an arid region made the collection and storage of water especially important. The city lay between seasonal streams whose water could be harnessed through a system of channels and reservoirs.

Dholavira is particularly significant because its surviving remains show how a Harappan settlement adapted its architecture to local environmental conditions. Stone, available in the surrounding region, was used extensively for walls and building foundations, distinguishing the site from settlements where brick construction predominated.

Multiple fortified sections

Dholavira is often described in textbooks as having 3 major urban divisions, unlike the simpler citadel–lower-town arrangement commonly associated with other Harappan cities. A more detailed description identifies a fortified castle with an associated bailey, a middle town, and a lower town, together with a ceremonial ground and other features.

Substantial stone walls and controlled gateways separated parts of the settlement. These divisions suggest planned differences in access and the organisation of urban space. However, the terms castle and bailey are modern archaeological descriptions; they do not establish the original Harappan names of those sections.

Public space and an unusual inscription

An extensive open area at Dholavira is interpreted as a ceremonial or public ground. Its presence shows that urban planning could provide space for gatherings in addition to houses and movement corridors.

Archaeologists also discovered an unusual arrangement of large Harappan signs made from white stone-like material. It is commonly described as a signboard. Most known Harappan inscriptions occur on much smaller objects, particularly seals. The Dholavira find is therefore important for understanding the possible public display of writing, although the signs themselves remain undeciphered.

Reservoirs and the use of seasonal water

Dholavira's water-management arrangements included channels, drains and large reservoirs. Some reservoirs were constructed using masonry, while others were cut into rock. At least 6 large reservoirs have been described in the Class 6 textbook account, and the longest reservoir cited there measured approximately 73 m in length.

Water storage helped the settlement meet its needs beyond periods of rainfall or stream flow. This was especially important in an environment without a dependable year-round supply from a large perennial river.

Archaeological significance and World Heritage status

The ruins demonstrate a combination of urban zoning, substantial stone construction and adaptation to a dry climate. The wider archaeological occupation of Dholavira is dated approximately 3000–1500 BCE in its World Heritage description; this must not be confused with the narrower Mature Harappan period of 2600–1900 BCE.

Dholavira: a Harappan City was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2021. As of the content cutoff of 23 November 2026, it is an inscribed World Heritage property, not merely a tentative proposal. Its conservation involves protecting the original stone structures, water-management remains and the archaeological setting in which they were found.

Prelims focus

  • Dholavira is on Khadir Bet in the Rann of Kutch, Gujarat.
  • The settlement had multiple fortified sections and extensive stone construction.
  • Its water system included large reservoirs and connecting channels.
  • An unusual large Harappan inscription was discovered at the site.
  • Dholavira was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2021.
  • Trap: Do not equate Dholavira's complete occupation period with the Mature Harappan period.

[Sources: NCERT, Our Pasts–I, Class 6, Chapter 4, In the Earliest Cities, p. 39; NCERT, Exploring Society: India and Beyond, Class 6, Chapter 6, The Beginnings of Indian Civilisation, pp. 91–96; UNESCO World Heritage Centre, Dholavira: a Harappan City, Description, Outstanding Universal Value and Inscription details, consulted 23 November 2026.]
